#!/bin/bash
# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables (unquoted slot),
# then reference them only as "$VAR" - never interpolate 
# inside a quoted context. See kubernetes_jq_query for the rationale.
KIND=pods
CUSTOM_COLUMNS='NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,IP:.status.podIP,PHASE:.status.phase,START:.status.startTime,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=boutique
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
FILTER_PATTERN=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""
[ "$FILTER_PATTERN" = "None" ] && FILTER_PATTERN=""

# kubectl ignores -n for cluster-scoped kinds; say so instead of reporting a namespace that wasn't applied
NOTES='[]'
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  is_kind() { awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind || index($1, kind ".") == 1 {found = 1} END {exit !found}'; }
  if kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind \
    && ! kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind; then
    NOTES=$(jq -nc --arg note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${KIND} is cluster-scoped." '[$note]')
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
fi

SCOPE_ARGS=()
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-n "$SEL_NAMESPACE")
else
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--all-namespaces)
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-l "$SEL_LABELS")
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--field-selector "$SEL_FIELDS")
fi

err_file=$(mktemp)
output=$(kubectl get "$KIND" "${SCOPE_ARGS[@]}" -o custom-columns="$CUSTOM_COLUMNS" 2>"$err_file")
kubectl_exit=$?
err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

SCOPE='null'
if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
    '{namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
      label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
      field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')
fi

if [ $kubectl_exit -ne 0 ] || [ -z "$output" ]; then
  if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
    jq -n --arg stderr "$err_content" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
      '{count: 0, header: null, rows: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  else
    echo "=== STDERR ==="
    echo "$err_content"
    echo "=== ROWS ==="
    echo "=== COUNT ==="
    echo 0
  fi
  exit 0
fi

# Split header and data rows
header=$(echo "$output" | head -1)
if [ -n "$FILTER_PATTERN" ]; then
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2 | grep -E -- "$FILTER_PATTERN" || true)
else
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2)
fi

if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then
    count=$(echo "$data" | wc -l)
  else
    count=0
  fi
  # Rows go through stdin, not --argjson, so large tables don't hit "Argument list too long"
  printf '%s' "$data" | jq -R . | jq -s \
    --argjson count "$count" \
    --arg header "$header" \
    --arg stderr "$err_content" \
    --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
    '{count: $count, header: $header, rows: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
else
  echo "=== STDERR ==="
  echo "$err_content"
  echo "=== HEADER ==="
  echo "$header"
  echo "=== ROWS ==="
  echo "$data"
  echo "=== COUNT ==="
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then echo "$data" | wc -l; else echo 0; fi
fi

#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=pods
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=diag-system
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, node: .spec.nodeName, hostNet: .spec.hostNetwork, containers: [.spec.containers[] | {name: .name, image: .image, priv: .securityContext.privileged, caps: .securityContext.capabilities, cmd: .command, args: .args, env: .env, mounts: .volumeMounts}], vols: .spec.volumes, phase: .status.phase}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then
  API_GROUPS=$(kubectl get --raw /apis 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.groups[].name' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Extract NAMESPACED value
if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Build API path: namespaced kinds can be listed within one namespace;
# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)
if [[ "$API_VERSION" == "v1" ]]; then
  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"
      fi
      MATCH_COUNT=$(echo "$MATCHES" | grep -c . || true)
      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

## 第 3 轮排查：对照前两轮的预期

### 一、被证实的（有新证据）

**1. 慢点在 currencyservice 的调用路径上，页面延迟 ≈ currency 调用次数 × 200ms**

刚取的 frontend 日志（`frontend-fd686dbb-xcmv8`，06:57:13–06:57:30，含 `http.resp.took_ms`）：

| 端点 | 每次请求的 currency RPC 数 | 实测 took_ms |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /` | 10–11 | 1999, 2108, 2121, 2131, 2173 |
| `GET /product/*` | 2 | 378, 387, 394, 395, 403, 405, 408, 411, 412, 416, 419, 420, 422, 424, 426, 429, 430, 432, 433, 436, 441, 443, 445, 447 |
| `GET /cart` | 2 × 条目数 | 393, 416, 579, 606, 612, 644, 650, 839, 847, 1043, 1254 |
| `POST /cart`（无 currency 调用） | 0 | **1, 2** |
| `/_healthz` | 0 | **0** |

**2. 延迟发生在「请求进入 currencyservice 之前」，响应方向是快的（这是本轮新获得的关键证据）**

把同一窗口内两边的毫秒时间戳对齐（currencyservice 的 `Getting supported currencies...` 是 handler 的第一条日志）：

```
06:57:45.4707 frontend "request started" GET /product/1YMWWN1N4O
06:57:45.664  currencyservice "Getting supported currencies..."   → +193ms
06:57:45.871  currencyservice "conversion request successful"     → +400ms（第2次RPC到达）
06:57:45.8759 frontend "request complete" took_ms=405
```
其余 8 个可干净配对的样本同样得到 +193 / +196 / +204 / +208 / +212 / +215 / +216 / +219 ms。

结论：**每个 RPC 的 ~200ms 全部花在「客户端已进入 handler → 服务端 handler 开始执行」这一段**，响应返回几乎不耗时。所以既不是 currencyservice 在处理里慢，也不是响应路径慢。而 round 1 曾等效地假设过「慢点在 currencyservice 一侧的网络或进程内」，本轮把它收窄为**单方向的入向延迟**。

**3. 规格层面全部是原版**：currencyservice `v0.10.3`、cpu limit 200m/request 100m/mem 128Mi、env 只有 `PORT=7000`+`DISABLE_PROFILER=1`；所有 Pod 单容器无 sidecar，无 `dnsConfig`/`hostAliases` 异常；EndpointSlice 正确（`currencyservice` 10.96.106.15:7000 → 唯一 ready 端点 10.244.0.111:7000，Pod `currencyservice-6df4cccbb9-s5xx4`）。

### 二、被推翻的

1. **round 2 的主假设「时延规则挂在未重建的客户端 Pod（frontend 10.244.0.103 / checkoutservice 10.244.0.101）的 netns 上」——推翻。** 这两个 Pod 已于 06:53:10 / 06:53:21 重建为 `frontend-fd686dbb-xcmv8`（10.244.0.113）和 `checkoutservice-5d5f4589c5-2s8nk`（10.244.0.114），之后数值毫无变化（中位 414ms，p90 2021ms）。同理 currencyservice 在 06:42:56 重建为新 IP 10.244.0.111 后也毫无变化。
   → 三种「Pod netns 内 tc 规则」的假设（currencyservice 出向、currencyservice 入向、客户端出向）**全部被三次重建排除**。这也是「重建 Pod 类操作」两轮都无效的原因：延迟根本不在这三个 netns 里。
2. **round 1 的「重启 currencyservice 即可恢复」——推翻**（结果已证实：无变化）。
3. **CPU/资源/进程内排队**——彻底排除：currencyservice 约 7 RPC/s，200m 配额（每 100ms 20ms）远未饱和；且若是 CFS 节流，`POST /cart`（同进程、1ms）不可能不受影响。
4. **adservice 是延迟原因**——再次确认不是：它毫秒级 `connection refused` 失败。

### 三、还没解释的

1. **规则挂在哪一层、按什么键匹配，我无法直接观测**：本 SA 无权 `get nodes`、无权 exec、也无法列出 `diag-system`/`kube-system` 的 Pod（都是 Forbidden），所以看不到节点上的 `tc qdisc/filter`、ifb 或 iptables 重定向。
2. 已排除「按 Pod IP 匹配」（Pod IP 换过，延迟不变）。剩下两个仍自洽、我无法区分的候选：
   - **按目的端口 7000 匹配**（入向 200ms，出向响应 dport 是临时端口，所以只有请求被延迟——与观测完全吻合）；
   - **按目的 ClusterIP 10.96.106.15:7000 匹配**（DNAT 前打标，同样只影响请求、且与 Pod 重建无关）。
   由于 currencyservice 的 liveness/readiness 探针写死 `grpc: 7000`，用「改 PORT + 改 targetPort 换端口绕开」会立刻让探针失败、Pod 变 NotReady、端点被摘除，会造成全量 500，不能采用。
3. **adservice 仍在 0 副本**：06:36:47 被删，上一轮 scale 到 1 在 06:53:23 建好 Pod、06:56:45 又被撤回到 0（`Scaled down replica-set adservice-6bfc5fc46c from 1 to 0`）。当前 frontend 仍在刷 `failed to retrieve ads: ... dial tcp 10.96.18.53:9555: connect: connection refused`（07:02 仍在发生，600 秒窗口内 497 条）。

# Investigation guidelines

* Gather data with as many tool calls as needed before responding; keep going until you reach the deepest root cause you can find.

A node condition does not tell you which pods it hit; a failing dependency does not tell you which of its clients broke; an unhealthy shared component does not mean its consumers are unhealthy. Check each entity before you name it, or do not name it — sampling a workload's replicas characterizes the WORKLOAD, so attribute what you found to it rather than to replicas you did not look at.

A pod that is 5 minutes old on a node that had trouble 5 minutes ago was not necessarily evicted — check what created it. Coincidence in time is not causation, and "also affected" is a claim that needs its own evidence.

If you cannot quote such a token for that entity, it does not go here — `SuccessfulDelete`, `SuccessfulCreate`, `Scheduled`, `Started` and a probe miss at startup are not among them. A recreation, restart or probe miss inside the window is never enough on its own, whatever sub-label you give it; **Checked, healthy** — you looked and found nothing wrong; **Changed during the window for another reason** — it restarted, was recreated or errored, and you name what did it (a controller rollout, a scheduled job, an operator, a probe at startup) and how you know; **Not checked**. messages.reasoning_content:
The tool seems to fail to display matched logs when the match count is small?? Maybe the matched logs come from the init container ("Multiple containers") — hmm, "Remaining: 0" after excluding nothing is a bug. Whatever; the failures (1.41%) are likely frontend 500s during the pod-restart windows (round 2 restarts at 06:53), which the user-side metric reported as 0 500s in its latest window.

Actually hold on, "GET /product/LS4PSXUNUM ... max 7139, 3 failures (1.90%)" — LS4PSXUNUM. Hmm, is that product in the catalog? If the frontend can't find the product → 500. Interesting: failures concentrated on some product IDs. But not relevant to latency.

Hmm, but it might matter: "GET / (3 failures 2.14%)". Let me not chase this; the user-side metric says 0 500s in the latest window and 0 failed orders. Locust's 1.41% might be from earlier windows (its stats are cumulative since start, including the chaos at 06:36-06:53).

Let me get back to the main question. I want one more piece of evidence to distinguish "delay inside currency process" vs "network into currency", because if the delay is *inside the currency process* (which we ruled out by pod recreation), fine. It's ruled out.

But here's a remaining alternative I should test: could the delay be **inside the frontend's gRPC client** (e.g., gRPC's name resolution / LB picking a *stale* subchannel)? Not with pod restarts... The frontend pod was recreated at 06:53 and the delay persisted. So the client process is fresh. So no.

OK wait. Hold on. Actually let me revisit something. What if the delay is in the **DNS resolution happening per-RPC** because both clients use `grpc.Dial` with... hmm, in the boutique frontend v0.10.3:

```go
func mustConnGRPC(ctx context.Context, conn **grpc.ClientConn, addr string) {
	var err error
	*conn, err = grpc.DialContext(ctx, addr, grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()), grpc.WithTimeout(time.Second*3))
```
Dial is non-blocking; the connection is established lazily on first RPC. Once established, resolution isn't repeated per RPC.

BUT — **what if the connection is in TRANSIENT_FAILURE repeatedly**? Then each RPC waits for reconnect. Reconnect would involve DNS + TCP. If DNS were slow (200ms), then... hmm! And a connection drop per RPC would be visible as errors? No — gRPC waits for a ready subchannel (wait-for-ready? default is fail-fast → would return UNAVAILABLE). We see no errors. Also the currencyservice logs show a continuous stream of arrivals, consistent with a single connection.

Hmm, but here's a thought: what would cause the *request* to take 200ms to arrive at the server but no errors and no reconnect... 

Let me consider the possibility of a **TCP window / delayed write** on the client side: gRPC-js server have small initial receive window? No: the server's TCP receive window is advertised; if the server's socket buffer is small/full, the client's send would be throttled. But the request is tiny.

I'm confident: netem-style delay on the request path.

Now, hmm, let me reconsider whether the delay could be **symmetric 100ms** but the handler log is at message decipher... no: total RPC = 200ms; if 100ms each way, the log would be at +100. We measured +193 to +219 for the *first* RPC. So asymmetric: ~200 request / ~0 response.

Interesting: an *asymmetric* delay suggests the qdisc is applied only on the direction toward the currencyservice (either at the source's egress with a port filter, or at the destination's ingress via ifb). A `netem delay` on a device's egress is standard; to delay ingress you need ifb redirection. The simplest implementation: `tc qdisc add dev <X> root netem delay 200ms` + a filter matching dport 7000. For this to catch requests (client→server) but not responses (server→client, dport=ephemeral), the device X must carry client→server traffic. Since the filter is by dport 7000, ANY device carrying that direction works. E.g. `cni0` root (host→pod egress for host-originated? no)...

Hmm, actually in a flannel/bridge setup, pod→pod traffic crosses the bridge internally via veth pairs; cni0's egress is used for host→pod. Both the client's pod egress (vethA, host-side ingress) and the server's ingress (vethB) are per-pod devices.

So where can a persistent-by-port rule live? An **ifb** device with redirect filters on all veths... but the redirect filters would also be per-device (destroyed on churn). Hmm.

Unless the delay is on the **node's eth0** (external interface): pod→pod traffic on the same node doesn't leave eth0. ✗.

Hmm!! So where?! Let me reconsider: maybe the rule IS in a pod netns but re-applied... 

Alternatively — what if it's implemented via **eBPF (TC/clsact) attached to the root cgroup** or via **`bpftool`-attached tc filters on the bridge device cni0**? 

Hmm, what about a tc filter attached to **`cni0`** with `prio` and `netem` on **cni0's root qdisc**, matching dport 7000? For pod→pod bridge traffic, does it egress via cni0? With a Linux bridge, no: the packet is forwarded between the bridge's ports directly (egress qdisc of the *port* device = vethB). Hmm, but wait: what device is vethB? In flannel+CNI bridge setups, the pod's veth peer is enslaved to the cni0 bridge; the port device IS the veth peer. So bridge forwarding = egress on the veth peer device. And cni0 is the bridge itself (a virtual device used for host traffic). So tc on cni0 affects only host-originated traffic.

Hmm, so how is the delay persistent?!

Unless the traffic is NOT bridged but *routed*: if the CNI is "ptp"-style (each pod gets a veth and routes via the host, no bridge), then pod→pod traffic goes: pod A → vethA → host routing → vethB. In that case a tc filter on **vethA's host-side ingress** would be per-pod (destroyed)... still.

Hmm, so maybe the delay IS in a pod netns and IS being re-applied by an agent on each new pod. That's the "injector re-applies by selector" scenario. In that case, no pod-level action helps — consistent with rounds 1 and 2 failing.

Wait... but is the CNI flannel-with-bridge? The pod names and 10.244.0.x with node name "tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane"; the events earlier showed nothing about CNI. Hmm.

BUT hold on — what if the delay isn't tc at all, and instead there's an agent doing something else? Let me look for evidence of the injector in the cluster: the `diag-system` namespace exists (my SA). Maybe there's a chaos agent there — I can't list pods cluster-wide (forbidden). Could I list pods in diag-system? My SA is in diag-system; permission may exist. Let me try listing pods in diag-system and any deployments/daemonsets there. That might reveal the injector and how it works — maybe even readable config (a ConfigMap listing the fault spec: delay 200ms on port 7000!). That would be great evidence. Worth trying: pods/deployments/daemonsets/configmaps in diag-system.

Let me try.

messages.reasoning_content:
Forbidden. So I can only see the boutique namespace (and limited kinds).

Let me check what I *can* do in boutique: services, pods, deployments, replicasets, endpointslices, events... maybe configmaps? Let me check for configmaps/secrets in boutique — unlikely to hold the fault.

Let me step back and consider the most defensible conclusion and best action for round 3.

Established facts (evidence-backed):
1. Delay ≈200ms per currency RPC, applied on the client→server direction, before the currencyservice handler is invoked (ms-level log correlation: "Getting supported currencies..." at +193…+219ms after frontend handler start; the 2nd RPC's arrival at +400ms with the page finishing at +405ms).
2. Latency ∝ number of currency RPCs: / (10-11 calls) 1999-2173ms; /product (2 calls) 378-447ms; /cart (2×items) 393-1254ms; POST /cart (0 currency calls) 1-2ms; /_healthz 0ms.
3. Ruled out: currencyservice pod/process (rebuilt 06:42:56, new IP 10.244.0.111, unchanged); client pods (frontend & checkoutservice rebuilt 06:53:10/06:53:21, unchanged); CPU limits/spec (vanilla, 200m/128Mi, upstream image); no sidecars, no injected env, no dnsConfig/hostAliases; Service/EndpointSlice correct (targetPort 7000 → 10.244.0.111:7000); no NetworkPolicy visible (forbidden), no chaos CRDs (round 2).
4. So the delay lives outside both endpoints — on the node's network path (tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane) or in a node-level agent/proxy, filtered to the currencyservice port 7000 / ClusterIP 10.96.106.15:7000, one direction only.

Also confirmed: only currency traffic is delayed — cart 7070 (POST /cart 1-2ms), productcatalog 3550, and currency responses are fast.

Round-2 hypotheses assessment:
- "rule in the surviving clients' netns" → REFUTED (both clients rebuilt, no change; also the delay is on the request direction, which even a client-side egress filter would explain... hmm, actually a client-side egress filter WOULD explain the direction. But the pods were rebuilt, so refuted).
- "node-level tc rule by port 7000" → still the leading explanation (survived all pod churn).

What remains unexplained: how the rule persists across pod churn — I could not get node/host access (nodes forbidden, no exec), so I cannot see the tc qdisc/filter, nor the injector (diag-system pods forbidden).

Now, about actions for round 3. I've argued for:
(a) scale adservice 1 — fixes the confirmed ad outage (0 replicas since 06:36:47, zero endpoints, "failed to retrieve ads ... connection refused").
(b) An attempt to route currency traffic around the delay.

For (b), is there a *better* attempt than pod IP? Let me think again...

Hmm hold on, wait. NEW IDEA! What if the delay is keyed on **port 7000** and we can dodge it by giving the clients a *different destination port on the same ClusterIP*... no.

But here's a cleverer variant: what if the *original* fault is keyed on the **ClusterIP 10.96.106.15**, and this ClusterIP is unchanged since before the incident. We could change what "currencyservice" resolves to by using the *frontend-external*-style... no.

Hmm, what about pointing clients at the **pod IP**? That's the only alternative address available.

Alternatively, what about pointing the clients at a *different service that happens to be a currency-compatible endpoint*? None.

So (b) = pod IP experiment.

Risk assessment for (b): 
- frontend & checkoutservice get `CURRENCY_SERVICE_ADDR=10.244.0.111:7000`, causing rollouts (~10s each). During rollout, one page-load could error. Acceptable.
- If successful: median drops to ~25ms, p90 ~40ms.
- If unsuccessful: numbers unchanged.
- Fragility: pod IP changes if currencyservice restarts.

Probability of success: depends on whether the filter matches the pre-DNAT dst (ClusterIP) rather than the port. Given the delay is asymmetric (request-only), a ClusterIP match would have to be pre-DNAT; a dport match works pre- or post-DNAT. I'd guess port-keyed is more likely (simpler), so maybe 25-35% success.

Hmm. Is there something with a higher success probability? Let me think about what else could cause a *persistent* asymmetric delay...

WAIT. WAIT. New thought: **what if the delay is on the currencyservice side but in the *host-to-pod* direction because of the pod's veth being throttled by... a *netem on the CNI bridge port* keyed to the pod's IP 10.244.0.111 — but the pod IP changed in round 1 (new pod → new IP), and the delay persisted.** Right, ruled out.

Hmm, what if the delay is keyed on the *node's* `eth0`, i.e., traffic routed through the node's default gateway? If the CNI is such that pod→pod traffic on the SAME node still goes out... no.

OK, hold on. Let me question one of my core measurements: is it possible that the first currency RPC is NOT the one logged at +193ms? What if the frontend calls getCurrencies and the request arrives *immediately*, but the Node app's log write is *buffered/delayed*? The log timestamps come from the app (winston with timestamp). Buffering doesn't change timestamp values.

Hmm, but WAIT: what if the *log timestamps* are generated at write-time... they're generated when the log call happens. Fine.

But hmm, what if the currencyservice's Node process's event loop is scheduled ~200ms late *per request* — i.e., every handler entry is delayed 200ms after socket data arrives? That's exactly "event loop blocked/idle-delayed". A pod restart (round 1) created a fresh process though, and the delay persisted. Unless the *image* is faulty... but it's the upstream image used by all (cartservice is .NET, shipping/payment/email are Go/Node?).

Hmm! Interesting: which services are Node? currencyservice (Node), paymentservice (Node), emailservice (Python), adservice (Java), cartservice (.NET), others Go. So paymentservice is also Node — if the *Node runtime* had an issue, paymentservice would be affected too. Order latency ~866ms avg — includes currency. Can't separate easily.

Anyway, the "process dispatch delay" hypothesis is refuted by round 1's pod recreation (new container, new process).

Hmm, unless... OH WAIT. Hmm! What if it's a **container image-level issue** with currencyservice only — but the pod restart re-pulls the same image → same behavior. That fits!! A *modified image* (e.g., a build with an injected 200ms sleep in the gRPC server interceptor, before the handler log!) would:
- persist across pod restarts ✓
- persist across client restarts ✓
- delay handler entry exactly ✓ (if the interceptor sleeps before calling the handler... but the log is the first line in the *handler*, so an interceptor delay would show up exactly as we see!)
- be one-directional (request side) ✓
- be specific to currencyservice ✓
- not involve network at all.

Hmm! But round 1 said "spec 为原版" and the image tag is `currencyservice:v0.10.3` — the standard upstream tag. Could someone have pushed a modified image with the same tag to that registry? That's "image tampering", possible but exotic. And *I can't compare digests* across services... Actually I can check `imageID` in pod status (the digest)! If the currencyservice image digest differs from what other v0.10.3 images look like... hmm, can't compare to upstream. But possibly all images share a common manifest digest pattern... no, different images.

Hmm, still, the interior-app hypothesis has a cheaper test: an app-level delay in the *handler* would show up differently: our correlation showed the delay BEFORE the handler log. An interceptor-based delay would be before the handler log — indistinguishable. Ugh.

But wait: is there any way to distinguish "delay inside the Node process before the handler" from "delay on the network before the process"? Hmm: yes! gRPC keepalive/probe traffic: the kubelet's gRPC health probe hits the *health service*, not the currency handlers. If it were an app-level interceptor, does the health service get intercepted? grpc-health-check service is registered on the same server, and an interceptor would apply. Can't measure it anyway.

Alternatively: **concurrency**. If a fixed 200ms sleep were added per request inside the process, the process could still handle many concurrently (Node async sleep) → arrivals at intervals consistent with the client's pacing. Our log interval analysis showed irregular intervals, consistent with both.

Hmm, so the "modified image / app-level sleep" hypothesis is alive. How to test with allowed ops? `set_env`? A sleep injected in code wouldn't be toggled by env... unless it's env-driven with a default! E.g., if someone built an image where `LATENCY_MS` default 200... no env present.

Hmm, what about DISABLE_PROFILER? no.

Hmm, so how to distinguish? Interesting idea: **the "Getting supported currencies..." log vs. the "conversion request successful" log for the SAME request**. If the sleep is *before* the handler (interceptor), then "Getting supported currencies..." → immediate response. If the sleep is *inside* the handler (e.g., before/after conversion), we'd see: arrival logged immediately, then "conversion request successful" 200ms later — and the response 200ms after arrival, which would mean the delay is on the response side, and then the first-RPC-arrival correlation (+193ms) wouldn't match. But it DID match (+193). So the sleep, if in-app, must be in an interceptor (before the handler) — an odd choice.

Hmm, so both remain: (i) network delay on the request path, (ii) an interceptor/queue before the handler in the app.

Now which one? Think about "how would a lab inject this fault?" A common approach in these fake-incident labs: they DO have a "fault injection" mechanism that patches deployments (env vars) or applies chaos. The op menu (set_env/unset_env) suggests the intended fix might be an env var on currencyservice... Hmm! But round 1 verified there are no non-standard env vars. Unless the injected env is on a *different* deployment!

OH. Hmm! What about the **frontend**'s env? `ENABLE_PROFILER=0`, `SHOPPING_ASSISTANT_SERVICE_ADDR=shoppingassistantservice:80` — note: there's NO `shoppingassistantservice` Service in the namespace (services list has no shoppingassistantservice!). But the frontend only calls it for the /assistant endpoint, which loadgenerator doesn't hit. Fine, pre-existing.

Hmm, so no injected env anywhere. All envs match upstream defaults (roughly).

OK so no env-based injection. So the fault was applied outside the pod specs: either node-level networking, or a modified image.

Hmm, hmm. Which? Let me look for more evidence on the *network* hypothesis: if packets to dport 7000 are delayed by 200ms each, then **TCP handshake** to currencyservice would also be delayed. The frontend establishes the connection at startup. Are there any reconnect events visible? The currencyservice logs show "Getting supported currencies" continuously with no gaps; if the connection dropped we'd see... nothing.

Alternatively, look at the *first* currency request after the frontend pod started (06:53:11) — it would include the connection setup. Not helpful.

Another discriminator: **packet-size/serialization**? no.

Another useful discriminator: does the delay apply to traffic into the *currencyservice Service* from a **non-boutique** client... unavailable.

What about the kubelet's gRPC probes on port 7000? If the delay applied to *all* packets to 7000, the kubelet probes (every 10s) would take 200ms+ and still pass. If it were an app interceptor, probes would also be delayed (health service intercepted). No discriminator, and we don't have probe latency data.

Hmm hm. What about the **number of packets**? A netem delay applies per packet; the RPC sends one small packet → 200ms. An app sleep → 200ms. Same.

OK, think about failure modes of each hypothesis given "the incident started at 06:36:47 while the adservice pod was being deleted (SuccessfulDelete at 06:36:47)". Wait: the adservice pod was deleted at 06:36:47 — that's the *scale-down* (or a delete). And the incident started then. Hmm, so both faults started at the same moment: 06:36:47ish. That's a strong hint that a single "chaos run" at 06:36:47 (a) scaled adservice to 0 and (b) applied the currency delay. A chaos tool that scales deployments = "chaos-mesh-like" but not chaos-mesh (no CRDs). A custom injector/script: `kubectl scale adservice --replicas=0` + something for the delay.

If the script did `tc qdisc add dev cni0 root netem delay 200ms` — that would delay ALL traffic on that device... which for pod→pod bridging affects... hmm, hmm! Actually wait. What if it ran `tc qdisc add dev cni0 root netem delay 200ms` and the CNI is a *routed* (ptp) setup where the pod subnet is reached via cni0 as a *routing* interface? Then all pod→pod traffic would be delayed 200ms... but cart is 1ms. So no.

What if the script ran `tc` inside the currencyservice pod's netns, then the pod restarted in round 1 → delay would be gone. It wasn't. So the script re-applies? Or the pod restart didn't happen... it did (new pod, new IP, new events).

Hmm, ok... so consider: what if the delay is applied **not by tc but by an iptables/eBPF rule keyed by cgroup**? no.

AGH. Let me look at this from another angle: What if the delay is applied at the **Service/EndpointSlice level** — e.g., the Service has an annotation... or the Service's port has... hmm. Actually! What about **`Service.spec.ports[].targetPort` pointing to something that adds latency**, like a port where a **sidecar-less** app... no.

What if there are TWO Services: `currencyservice` (10.96.106.15) and maybe the frontend resolves `currencyservice` to a different IP via **CoreDNS rewrite/hosts injection**? CoreDNS corefile could have a `hosts` block mapping currencyservice → some IP! Hmm, but the packets DO reach the currencyservice pod (we see the requests logged). So the destination is right.

OK. Let me try yet another discriminator for network-vs-app: the **timing distribution's relationship to client pacing**. Under a network delay of exactly 200ms, the arrival at the server = send + 200 exactly, with jitter from the kernel. Under an app-level sleep, arrival = send + ssleep (200) + scheduling. Both similar.

Hmm, what about the asymmetry of jitter: measured 182, 193, 196, 204, 208, 212, 215, 216, 219. Both directions of jitter (below and above 200). netem with no jitter would be 200 + fixed kernel overhead (usually exactly 200-202ms, consistent small positive bias). We see 182 (18ms *less* than 200) — that's impossible for a delay of 200ms WITHOUT jitter unless my timestamp pairing is off by which request matched (concurrency). Given concurrency, my matches could be wrong by ±. The 182 case (cart at 49.4089 → 49.591) may have been mispaired. Meh.

Another thought: is the delay maybe 100ms in each direction (netem on both sides, or delay on the pod's veth both ways), i.e., true RTT 200ms, and the server-side log at +100? We measured +193..+219, i.e., ~200 not ~100. So no.

Hmm, hold on! That's an important point actually. Let's reconsider: if netem delay were applied to the currencyservice pod's veth *egress* only (typical chaos-mesh style: `tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms` inside the pod's netns), the delay affects the pod's OUTGOING packets (responses). Then the server logs "Getting" immediately at client send (+0) and the response arrives at client at +200. Under that, my correlation would show the first "Getting" log at ~+0ms, and the *page* would still take 400ms (2 RPCs × 200 response delay). But I measured +193ms. That rules out the response-side delay decisively → confirms the delay is on the *request* direction. Good — and that's exactly why round 1's restart of currencyservice pod was never going to help if the rule was in its netns egress... wait, if the rule were in the currencyservice pod netns (egress=response), then restarting the pod WOULD have removed it. It didn't help. So the rule isn't in its netns at all. Combined with the request-direction finding, the delay is on the *ingress* side of the currencyservice traffic, applied outside its netns → on the client side (egress) or on the host path.

And the client side was recreated in round 2 → so it's the HOST path.
